source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Corn requires large amounts of potassium to support development of its root system, stalk, and ears, and to raise yield. Potassium is not lost from the soil as easily as nitrogen. It is generally concentrated in the stalks and roots of the corn plant, which means burning crop residue after harvest causes significant loss of nutrients — particularly potassium and phosphorus. Corn takes up potassium from the soil in its ionic (K+) form.

Symptoms of potassium deficiency: weak overall growth with thin stalks; young leaves appear dull green while older leaves die back quickly; and yield drops sharply when the crop is potassium-deficient.

Correction: select a fertilizer with high potassium content and apply it before or during planting. Potassium fertilizer such as muriate of potash (KCl, potassium chloride) can burn/rot the seed or seedling if it comes into direct contact, so it should be placed a short distance away from the seed rather than touching it. Ploughing crop residue back into the soil is described as necessary for boosting organic-matter content, especially potassium.
